records.title: Mombasa–Nairobi SGR: railway service and receiving networks
records.answer: The Mombasa–Nairobi standard-gauge railway links the coast with inland passenger and freight terminals. Its operating story depends on service patterns, cargo handling and connections beyond the main line.
records.scope: The 472-kilometre Mombasa–Nairobi Phase 1 railway, counted once. Excludes the separate Nairobi–Suswa/Naivasha Phase 2A extension, future western extensions, the older metre-gauge system and the entire Northern Corridor as additional identities.
records.stage: Passenger and commercial freight operation documented; new vehicle-haulage movement reported. No independent safety, financial-return or recurring Phase 1 performance admission.

identity_decision.rationale: A geographically bounded and named railway project linking Mombasa and Nairobi is supported by operator opening and service records. Its passenger and freight uses are one identity, while later extensions and receiving facilities remain dependencies. No existing historical acquisition docket is reused.

timeline.event: Passenger inauguration described in the operator's later retrospective.
Commercial freight operations began, distinct from passenger inauguration.
Separate Nairobi transit shed inaugurated as a receiving-system dependency.
Eight-year operating ceremony, reported June 13; cumulative service figures retain their scope.
Inaugural vehicle-haulage train described in the November 2 announcement.

sections.heading: One railway phase with two service roles
sections.text: Kenya Railways describes the Mombasa–Nairobi standard-gauge railway as a 472-kilometre line. Its retrospective records the passenger inauguration on May 31, 2017 and the start of commercial freight operations on January 1, 2018. These are distinct service milestones on one railway, not two projects. The later Nairobi–Suswa extension belongs to Phase 2A and remains outside this account's counted identity. Keeping the first phase separate makes comparisons more useful: an extension can change network reach and aggregate traffic without changing the geographic scope of the original project.

sections.heading: Different trains serve different journeys
sections.text: The operator advertises inter-county, afternoon and night services between the two termini. The inter-county pattern includes intermediate stations, while the other patterns make fewer stops. A separate Suswa leisure service uses the extension beyond Nairobi. These distinctions matter to access: an end-to-end traveller and a passenger boarding at an intermediate town do not receive the same offer. The published service description is not a record of trains actually run or observed punctuality. Journey assessment should include reaching the terminus and onward travel, rather than equating station-to-station time with a household's whole trip.

sections.heading: Vehicle haulage adds a new freight use
sections.text: A November 2, 2026 announcement reports that the inaugural vehicle-haulage train left the Port of Mombasa on October 29 and reached the Embakasi inland depot within eight hours. It carried 21 vehicles on four specially fabricated carriers alongside container wagons. Kenya Railways separately states a target of 700 vehicles per month. The first movement establishes a reported service milestone; the monthly target is not achieved volume. This distinction also matters for reliability: one reported journey cannot establish the repeated transit time or availability that a vehicle importer would need for regular planning.

sections.heading: Receiving facilities shape the logistics offer
sections.text: The Nairobi transit shed is a separate customs-approved temporary storage and cargo-deconsolidation facility in the central business district. Kenya Railways dates its inauguration to November 10, 2020 and describes capacity of up to 1,000 twenty-foot-equivalent units. That is stated capacity, not measured throughput. The shed is intended to bring handling closer to small and medium traders and complement the inland container depot. It illustrates why a main railway's usefulness depends on storage, customs processes, consolidators and local distribution. The operator's claimed savings would require their own comparable cost and waiting-time evidence.

sections.heading: Read cumulative operating totals carefully
sections.text: The operator's June 2025 anniversary account reports more than 15.3 million passengers and 39.78 million tonnes of cargo over the Madaraka Express operating history. These are cumulative service totals, not a Phase 1-only annual series or a count of unique people. The same account describes additional coaches, freight wagons and a predominantly Kenyan workforce, showing that the operating system continues to change after construction. Its celebratory safety and economic language remains the operator's assessment. Comparable evaluation needs reporting boundaries that separate the original line, extensions and service types across the same periods.

sections.heading: Follow the complete passenger and freight journey
sections.text: The next edition should pair railway operations with the connections and handling steps that users actually encounter. Passenger reporting needs cancellations, delay distributions and accessible onward travel by service pattern. Freight reporting needs terminal dwell time, delivery reliability and total handling cost for defined cargo types. Financial assessment should separate operating costs, capital financing and public support rather than infer viability from cumulative traffic. These evidence requests keep the project useful as a transport-system case while preserving the distinction between a completed asset, an advertised service and a sustained result.

next_artifacts: Comparable Phase 1 passenger and freight reporting with stable periods and route boundaries.
Vehicle-haulage operating volumes and transit-time distributions after the inaugural movement.
Terminal dwell-time, complete journey cost and financial accounts separating operations from capital financing.

records.title: Nairobi City County: mobility and neighbourhood services
records.answer: Nairobi’s county account connects a new transit framework with neighbourhood facilities, school meals and digital access. Each service has its own delivery stage and geographic reach.
records.scope: Nairobi City County, County 047, as one administrative place. Not the wider Nairobi metropolitan commuter area, neighbouring counties or every territory served by a Nairobi-named institution.
records.stage: County identity, reported local facilities and service programmes documented; transit implementation framework approved. No operating NMRTS network or countywide causal outcome admission.

identity_decision.rationale: The Council of Governors identifies Nairobi City County as County 047, while dated county and intergovernmental accounts locate services within named neighbourhoods and wards. The county is one place, not a sum of programme sites or the larger metropolitan region. No historical country docket is repurposed.

timeline.event: County formation year described by the Council of Governors profile; no exact day inferred.
Separate neighbourhood-facility and school-meal accounts published; not an opening date for every site.
Jericho hub launch account published; the exact opening day is not supplied.
County Executive approved the NMRTS Phase I implementation framework.

sections.heading: Use the county rather than the metropolitan label
sections.text: The Council of Governors identifies Nairobi as County 047 and describes its formation in 2013 on the former provincial boundaries. This account uses that administrative place, not every settlement whose residents commute to Nairobi. The distinction is important when transport plans refer to a metropolitan network while other services are organised by wards, schools or neighbourhoods. A county profile can connect those responsibilities without adding their populations together. Its boundary also prevents regional transport ambitions from being read as benefits already received by every county resident or by neighbouring communities.

sections.heading: A transit framework is a delivery decision
sections.text: On July 22, 2026, the County Executive announced approval of the implementation framework for Phase I of the Nairobi Metropolitan Mass Rapid Transit System. The proposal centres on a CBD underground core and an Eastlands line, with connections to bus rapid transit and pedestrian access. The announcement places public participation and implementation preparation ahead of groundbreaking. It therefore documents a framework decision, not an operating underground railway. The intended travel-time, cost and emissions improvements are objectives whose delivery will depend on design, funding, construction and the connections passengers can actually use.

sections.heading: Neighbourhood facilities combine several everyday needs
sections.text: A September 2025 Council of Governors account describes public sanitation, community kitchens, digital facilities and play spaces under the Urban Fabric Initiative within KISIP II. In Kayole Soweto it reports a social hall, water purifier, washrooms, study room and computer lab. Other named sites still had works underway in the same account. This combination shows how neighbourhood infrastructure can support study, hygiene and social activity together. The reported facilities in Kayole and Kahawa Soweto should not be extended into a claim that every KISIP II site is complete or offers the same continuing service.

sections.heading: School meals link daily logistics with education
sections.text: The Council of Governors' September 4, 2025 account reports that Dishi na County had served 50 million meals over two years. It describes 17 central kitchens preparing food for distribution to public primary schools, with expansion to informal schools still planned. Meals are repeated service units, not 50 million different learners. The account also attributes improvements in attendance and learning to the programme, but does not provide a comparison design establishing those effects. A stronger assessment would retain the delivery record while examining who receives meals, continuity, affordability and educational outcomes separately.

sections.heading: A local digital hub is not citywide coverage
sections.text: An October 27, 2025 account reports the launch of the Jericho Incubation Hub in Harambee Ward, Makadara. The partnership combines the county, Computer Aid Kenya and supporting technology and training organisations. Its intended offer includes digital literacy, startup support, mentoring and children's coding activities. The named location makes the initiative more concrete than a general smart-city ambition, but the plan to reach all 85 wards is not 85 operating hubs. Continued usefulness depends on access, equipment, staffing and participation; the launch account does not establish sustained employment gains for users.

sections.heading: Compare service reach and continuity
sections.text: The next update should show how residents encounter these services across the county, including neighbourhoods not yet reached. Transit needs actual delivery milestones and usable interchanges. Community facilities need opening hours, maintenance and participation records. Meals need comparable delivery and learner-level measures, while digital hubs need evidence of sustained access and training completion. These questions allow a place account to examine unequal service reach without collapsing everything into one score. They also keep a local milestone visible when a wider programme remains incomplete or its outcome evidence is still developing.

next_artifacts: NMRTS participation, funding and construction records followed by actual service milestones.
Named neighbourhood-facility continuity and maintenance records, separating completed sites from ongoing works.
School-meal and digital-hub participation and outcome evidence with stable denominators and credible comparisons.

records.title: Mombasa County: local access and water-service dependencies
records.answer: Mombasa’s place account connects coastal transport gateways with walking, commuter rail and household water services. Large corridors and local networks have different responsibilities and delivery stages.
records.scope: Mombasa County as one administrative place, including its island and mainland areas. Excludes neighbouring Kilifi and Kwale counties, the whole Northern Corridor and the port's international trading catchment.
records.stage: County administrative scope and local-service responsibilities documented; station construction progress and a historical water-repair notice retained. No station opening, continuous-water guarantee or countywide outcome admission.

identity_decision.rationale: The county's development plan defines six named sub-counties and an administrative territory distinct from neighbouring counties and regional transport catchments. Department, utility and railway records locate different services within that place. These are evidence for one county profile, not additional counted projects or a synthetic performance score.

timeline.event: Mombasa–Nairobi passenger inauguration provides regional-connection context.
Start year of the 2023–2027 plan period, not an asserted publication or adoption day.
Utility issued a West mainland repair-interruption notice; restoration time was not observed.
Separate Changamwe station construction percentages reported; end-November completion remained forecast.

sections.heading: The county includes island and mainland communities
sections.text: Mombasa's Third County Integrated Development Plan identifies six sub-counties: Mvita, Nyali, Changamwe, Jomvu, Kisauni and Likoni. The county borders Kilifi, Kwale and the Indian Ocean. This administrative frame includes more than the island or the port itself, while remaining smaller than the transport corridor and commercial catchments it serves. The 2023–2027 label is the plan period, not a claim that all proposed work is complete. Keeping the county boundary clear helps locate local service responsibilities without assigning neighbouring communities or every port user to Mombasa's resident population.

sections.heading: Walking and street management are part of connectivity
sections.text: The county transport department lists roads, lighting, traffic management and public transport among its responsibilities. Its account describes pedestrian walkways and cycle parking, alongside planned traffic-system improvements. These local elements connect people to jobs, shops and larger transport services; a regional gateway still requires a usable last part of the journey. The department's mandate distinguishes county transport from international and national shipping regulation. Its facility descriptions are not a direct observation of accessibility or safety performance, so a completed walkway should be followed through its crossings, maintenance and everyday use.

sections.heading: Commuter stations were still under construction
sections.text: Kenya Railways' October 19, 2026 update reports Changamwe East at 52 percent complete and Changamwe West at 38 percent. These are separate station figures, not a combined completion rate. The intended service would connect nearby communities with commuter rail and the Mombasa SGR terminus, supported by park-and-ride facilities. Completion by the end of November was a forecast in that account, not an opening record. This illustrates a local access dependency: an established intercity railway does not mean every proposed feeder station is already available to passengers.

sections.heading: Water service involves more than a connection
sections.text: MOWASSCO describes its role as providing water and sanitation services to Mombasa residents, billing customers and maintaining infrastructure. Its connection-service page explains how new premises enter that system. A connection, an account and routine maintenance are related but different parts of service provision. They do not establish that water reaches every connected home continuously. The useful place-level question is how the provider's network and maintenance responsibilities translate into reliable access in particular neighbourhoods. That assessment needs supply and interruption records, rather than treating the existence of a connection procedure as a household outcome.

sections.heading: A repair notice reveals a bulk-supply dependency
sections.text: On March 18, 2025, MOWASSCO announced an approximately 72-hour interruption in West mainland areas while the Coast Water Works Development Agency repaired a major leak on the Mzima pipeline. The notice named Miritini, Mikindani, Jomvu, Changamwe and Magongo, and anticipated resumption according to the distribution schedule after repairs. This is a historical notice, not evidence of present conditions. The announced duration is not observed restoration time. It nonetheless identifies a concrete dependency between the retail utility, a bulk-water provider and neighbourhood supply, which a meaningful continuity record should follow through to actual recovery.

sections.heading: Track access from the gateway to the household
sections.text: Further reporting should join local travel and water-service evidence without pretending they share one performance measure. For transport, follow the two stations separately through acceptance, opening and usable connections, then examine pedestrian access around them. For water, connect interruption notices to dated restoration, scheduled supply and neighbourhood experience. The county plan supplies a spatial frame; operator and utility records supply different parts of the service history. Keeping those roles distinct will make comparisons more useful than a broad claim that regional infrastructure has automatically solved local access or reliability.

next_artifacts: Separate acceptance and opening records for Changamwe East and West, followed by actual connecting services.
Pedestrian access and maintenance evidence around stations and everyday destinations.
Dated water-restoration and distribution records tied to specific neighbourhoods and bulk-supply incidents.
